name: Vedic Saṃhitās
summary: The four mantra collections — Ṛgveda, Sāmaveda, Yajurveda (Śukla and Kṛṣṇa) and Atharvaveda — that form the base of the Vedic canon and were transmitted orally by recitation schools (śākhās).
details:
Each Saṃhitā belongs to one or more schools (śākhās) that also transmitted a Brāhmaṇa, and often an Āraṇyaka and Upaniṣad; in the traditional wide sense “Veda” covers this whole sequence Saṃhitā → Brāhmaṇa → Āraṇyaka → Upaniṣad. Scholars (e.g. Witzel) distinguish a Ṛgvedic period, a Mantra period (Atharvaveda, Sāmaveda, Yajurveda mantras), a period of Yajurveda Saṃhitā prose, the Brāhmaṇa period, and the late Vedic Upaniṣads and Sūtras.

Transmission was oral and remains so in living recitation lineages. UNESCO recognised the “Tradition of Vedic chanting” (India): proclaimed in 2003 and inscribed on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2008; UNESCO notes that only thirteen of over a thousand recitation branches survive. Written manuscripts are late (second millennium CE).

name: Brāhmaṇas
summary: Prose texts attached to each Vedic school that explain the meaning, origin and correct performance of the śrauta rites, often through myths (ākhyāna) and identifications (bandhu).
details: Examples: Aitareya and Kauṣītaki (Ṛgveda); Pañcaviṃśa/Tāṇḍya and Jaiminīya (Sāmaveda); Taittirīya and Śatapatha (Yajurveda); Gopatha (Atharvaveda). Several first narrate stories later retold in the epics and Purāṇas: the flood of Manu (ŚB 1.8.1), the dwarf Viṣṇu winning the earth (ŚB 1.2.5), Purūravas and Urvaśī (ŚB 11.5.1), Śunaḥśepa (AB 7.13–18). Witzel places the main Brāhmaṇa period roughly in the early first millennium BCE, before the Upaniṣads.

name: Āraṇyakas
summary: Late Vedic texts, studied apart from the village, that treat esoteric or dangerous rites (e.g. the Pravargya) and contain or shade into the oldest Upaniṣads.
details: The Aitareya Āraṇyaka contains the Aitareya Upaniṣad (AĀ 2.4–6); the Kauṣītaki (Śāṅkhāyana) Āraṇyaka contains the Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad; the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka contains the Taittirīya Upaniṣad (TĀ 7–9) and the Mahānārāyaṇa Upaniṣad (TĀ 10); the Bṛhadāraṇyaka (“great Āraṇyaka”) forms the last part of the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa. These embeddings are the textual basis for the layered sequence Saṃhitā → Brāhmaṇa → Āraṇyaka → Upaniṣad.

sources.locator: Introduction (the Upaniṣads within the Vedic corpus)

name: Upaniṣads
summary: Texts at the end of the Vedic corpus (hence “Vedānta”) that discuss the self (ātman), brahman, death and rebirth, and liberation; the principal (“early”) Upaniṣads number about thirteen.
details:
Olivelle’s relative chronology: the prose Bṛhadāraṇyaka and Chāndogya are the oldest and pre-Buddhist (c. 7th–6th c. BCE, give or take a century); Taittirīya, Aitareya and Kauṣītaki follow (c. 6th–5th c. BCE); the verse Upaniṣads — Kena (the earliest of them), Kaṭha, Īśā, Śvetāśvatara, Muṇḍaka — belong to the last few centuries BCE; Praśna and Māṇḍūkya cannot be much older than the beginning of the common era. Olivelle warns that dating closer than a few centuries is unstable. Hundreds of later works also call themselves Upaniṣads.

The Upaniṣads, the Bhagavad Gītā and the Brahma Sūtra form the “triple foundation” (prasthānatrayī) on which Vedānta schools, including Advaita, write commentaries.

name: Vedāṅgas
summary: The six “limbs of the Veda” — phonetics (śikṣā), ritual (kalpa), grammar (vyākaraṇa), etymology (nirukta), metre (chandas) and astronomy/calendar (jyotiṣa) — developed to preserve, understand and apply the Vedic texts.
details: The six are listed together in Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 1.1.5, which classes the four Vedas and these six disciplines as the “lower knowledge” (aparā vidyā). Representative works: the Prātiśākhyas and Śikṣās (phonetics), the Kalpa Sūtras (ritual), Pāṇini’s Aṣṭādhyāyī (grammar), Yāska’s Nirukta (etymology), Piṅgala’s Chandaḥsūtra (metre) and the Vedāṅga Jyotiṣa.

name: Kalpa Sūtras
summary: Aphoristic manuals of each Vedic school that codify the solemn (śrauta) rites, domestic (gṛhya) rites, rules of conduct (dharma) and altar geometry (śulba).
details: Well-known sets belong to Āpastamba, Baudhāyana and Hiraṇyakeśin (Taittirīya school), Āśvalāyana and Śāṅkhāyana (Ṛgveda), Kātyāyana (Śukla Yajurveda) and others. The Śrauta Sūtras are the operative manuals of living śrauta performances; the Dharma Sūtras precede the metrical Dharmaśāstras such as the Manusmṛti (`text:manusmriti`). Dating is debated; the older Sūtras are usually placed in the last centuries BCE.

name: Rigveda
summary: The oldest Vedic collection: 1,028 hymns in ten books (maṇḍalas) addressed chiefly to Indra, Agni and Soma, composed by hereditary poet families and transmitted orally with exceptional fidelity.
details:
Structure (checked against Aufrecht’s text on GRETIL): ten maṇḍalas of 191, 43, 62, 58, 87, 75, 104, 103 (incl. the eleven Vālakhilya hymns 8.49–59), 114 and 191 hymns — 1,028 in all, 10,552 verses. The “family books” 2–7 are each attributed to one poet clan (Gṛtsamada, Viśvāmitra, Vāmadeva, Atri, Bharadvāja, Vasiṣṭha) and form the oldest layer; maṇḍala 9 gathers all hymns to Soma Pavamāna; maṇḍalas 1 and 10 (191 hymns each) are later collections, maṇḍala 10 containing the late cosmogonic hymns (10.90, 10.121, 10.129) and dialogue hymns (10.10, 10.95, 10.108).

Only the Śākala recension survives complete; Śākalya’s word-by-word padapāṭha and the more complex recitation patterns (krama, jaṭā, ghana) protected the text in oral transmission, which UNESCO recognised (2003/2008). The oldest surviving manuscripts are of the 11th century CE (Nepal, per Witzel); the BORI collection in Pune (`ms:rigveda-bori`, owned by the material agent) was placed on UNESCO’s Memory of the World Register in 2007. Sāyaṇa’s 14th-century commentary is the standard traditional exegesis.

name: Samaveda
summary: The Veda of chants (sāman): verses, almost all drawn from the Ṛgveda, arranged for singing by the udgātṛ priests in the soma rites, with separate song-books (gāna) recording the melodies.
details: Three recensions are known: Kauthuma, Rāṇāyanīya and Jaiminīya. Its Brāhmaṇas include the Pañcaviṃśa (Tāṇḍya) and Jaiminīya; the Chāndogya Upaniṣad belongs to the Kauthuma school and the Kena Upaniṣad to the Jaiminīya (Jaiminīya Upaniṣad Brāhmaṇa). It is commonly stated that all but about 75 of its verses occur in the Ṛgveda (recall; check against an edition).

name: Yajurveda
summary: The Veda of sacrificial formulas (yajus) recited by the adhvaryu priest who performs the manual acts of the rite; it exists in a “Black” (Kṛṣṇa) branch mixing mantra and explanatory prose and a “White” (Śukla) branch with mantras alone.
details: Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda Saṃhitās: Taittirīya, Maitrāyaṇī, Kāṭhaka and Kapiṣṭhala-Kaṭha. Śukla Yajurveda: the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā in Mādhyandina and Kāṇva recensions, with the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa. Upaniṣads of the branch include the Bṛhadāraṇyaka and Īśā (Śukla) and the Taittirīya, Kaṭha and Śvetāśvatara (Kṛṣṇa).

name: Śukla Yajurveda (Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā)
summary: The “White” Yajurveda, the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā in forty chapters (Mādhyandina and Kāṇva recensions), whose mantras are separated from the explanatory prose collected in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa.
details: Tradition, already in Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.5.3, attributes these “white formulas” to Yājñavalkya Vājasaneya. Notable chapters: VS 16 (the Śatarudriya, parallel to TS 4.5), VS 31 (a version of the Puruṣa hymn) and VS 40 (= the Īśā Upaniṣad). Witzel associates the school with the eastern, Videha region in the late Vedic period.

name: Taittirīya Saṃhitā (Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda)
summary: The principal Saṃhitā of the Black Yajurveda, in seven books (kāṇḍas) mixing ritual formulas with Brāhmaṇa-style prose explanation; it contains the Śatarudrīya litany to Rudra (TS 4.5).
details: The Taittirīya school, with its Brāhmaṇa, Āraṇyaka (incl. the Taittirīya Upaniṣad) and the Āpastamba, Baudhāyana and Hiraṇyakeśin Sūtras, is the most widely transmitted Yajurveda school in South India. TS 4.5 (eleven anuvākas, “namas te rudra manyave …”) and 4.7 (Camaka) are recited as the Śrī Rudram–Camakam in Śaiva worship.

name: Atharvaveda
summary: The fourth Veda, a collection of hymns and spells for healing, protection, prosperity, love, kingship and domestic life, alongside speculative cosmological hymns; preserved in the Śaunaka and Paippalāda recensions.
details: The Śaunaka Saṃhitā has twenty books (about 730 hymns); books 19–20 are later supplements, book 20 consisting largely of Ṛgvedic hymns to Indra plus the Kuntāpa hymns (which praise a king Parikṣit). The Paippalāda recension survives in Kashmiri and Orissan manuscript traditions. Upaniṣads of this Veda include the Muṇḍaka, Praśna and Māṇḍūkya; its Brāhmaṇa is the Gopatha.

name: Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa
summary: The Brāhmaṇa of the White Yajurveda, the largest and most systematic Brāhmaṇa (“of a hundred paths”), and a source of many narratives later retold in the epics and Purāṇas.
details: Mādhyandina recension: 14 kāṇḍas (100 adhyāyas); a Kāṇva recension also exists. Books 1–5 often cite Yājñavalkya, books 6–10 (the fire-altar) Śāṇḍilya; book 14 ends with the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad. Passages checked on GRETIL for this dataset include: the flood of Manu (1.8.1), the dwarf Viṣṇu who wins the earth for the gods (1.2.5), “yajño vai viṣṇuḥ” (1.1.2.13), Videgha Māthava and the eastward course of Agni Vaiśvānara (1.4.1.10–17), Rudra left behind by the gods (1.7.3.1), the eight names of the new-born Kumāra/Rudra (6.1.3.7–18), Purūravas and Urvaśī (11.5.1), Janaka’s sacrifice (11.6.3), the aśvamedha kings Janamejaya Pārikṣita and Bharata Dauḥṣanti, son of Śakuntalā (13.5.4), Puruṣa Nārāyaṇa’s five-night sacrifice (13.6.1.1) and the beheading of Viṣṇu (14.1.1).

name: Aitareya Brāhmaṇa
summary: A Ṛgvedic Brāhmaṇa for the hotṛ priest in forty adhyāyas (eight pañcikās), best known for the royal consecration (rājasūya) material and the story of Śunaḥśepa (AB 7.13–18).
details: The Śunaḥśepa narrative (pañcikā 7, khaṇḍas 13–18 = adhyāya 33) is recited to the consecrated king in the rājasūya. Keith regarded books 1–5 as older than books 6–8. Sāyaṇa commented on it; Keith translated it (HOS 25, 1920).

name: Taittirīya Āraṇyaka
summary: The Āraṇyaka of the Taittirīya school in ten prapāṭhakas; books 7–9 are the Taittirīya Upaniṣad and book 10 the Mahānārāyaṇa Upaniṣad.
details: Includes material on the Pravargya and on the creation and cosmology; its embedded Upaniṣads show the gradual transition from Āraṇyaka to Upaniṣad.

dates.label: c. 7th–3rd c. BCE (broad; TĀ 10 later)
dates.basis: relative chronology of Taittirīya texts

name: Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad
summary: The largest and, with the Chāndogya, the oldest Upaniṣad, forming the end of the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa; it presents Yājñavalkya’s teachings at Janaka’s court, his dialogues with Maitreyī and Gārgī, and the earliest explicit doctrine of karma and rebirth.
details: Six adhyāyas in Kāṇva and Mādhyandina recensions: the Madhu-kāṇḍa (1–2), the Yājñavalkya-kāṇḍa (3–4) and supplements (5–6), each section closing with teacher lineages (vaṃśa). Key passages verified on GRETIL: 1.4 (the self alone in the beginning; “ahaṃ brahmāsmi” 1.4.10), 2.3.6 (“neti neti”), 2.4 and 4.5 (Maitreyī), 3.1–9 (the contest at Janaka’s sacrifice, incl. Gārgī 3.6 and 3.8), 3.2.13 and 4.4.5–6 (karma), 6.2 (Pravāhaṇa Jaivali’s doctrine of the two paths), 6.3.7 (Uddālaka Āruṇi teaches Yājñavalkya) and 6.5.3 (the “white” formulas of Yājñavalkya Vājasaneya). Śaṅkara’s commentary on it is accepted as authentic.

name: Chāndogya Upaniṣad
summary: An early prose Upaniṣad of the Kauthuma Sāmaveda school, in eight prapāṭhakas, containing Uddālaka Āruṇi’s instruction of Śvetaketu (“tat tvam asi”), the “five fires” doctrine of rebirth, and the only Vedic mention of a Kṛṣṇa son of Devakī (3.17.6).
details: Verified passages: 1.1.1 (meditation on Om as the udgītha), 3.14.1 (“sarvaṃ khalv idaṃ brahma”, Śāṇḍilya), 3.17.6 (Ghora Āṅgirasa teaches Kṛṣṇa Devakīputra), 4.4 (Satyakāma Jābāla), 5.3–10 (Pravāhaṇa Jaivali and the five fires; rebirth according to conduct 5.10.7), 6.1–16 (Uddālaka and Śvetaketu; “tat tvam asi” nine times from 6.8.7), 7.1.1 (Nārada approaches Sanatkumāra), 8.7–12 (Indra and Virocana as pupils of Prajāpati).

name: Taittirīya Upaniṣad
summary: Books 7–9 of the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka, in three vallīs (Śikṣā, Brahmānanda, Bhṛgu), known for the five sheaths of the self and Varuṇa’s instruction of his son Bhṛgu on brahman.

name: Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad
summary: A Ṛgvedic Upaniṣad in four chapters, part of the Kauṣītaki (Śāṅkhāyana) Āraṇyaka, in which kṣatriya teachers instruct brahmins: Citra Gāṅgyāyani teaches Āruṇi, Indra teaches Pratardana, and Ajātaśatru teaches Bālāki.

name: Kena Upaniṣad
summary: A short Upaniṣad of the Jaiminīya Sāmaveda school: two verse sections on the unknowable brahman, followed by the prose parable in which Agni, Vāyu and Indra fail to recognise a mysterious being until Umā Haimavatī reveals that it is brahman.
details: Four khaṇḍas (checked in the Sanskrit Documents e-text): 1–2 in verse, 3–4 in prose. It forms part of the Jaiminīya Upaniṣad Brāhmaṇa (traditionally JUB 4.18–21; recall). Olivelle regards it as the oldest of the verse Upaniṣads.

name: Kaṭha Upaniṣad
summary: A verse Upaniṣad in six vallīs framed by the story of the boy Naciketas, who receives three boons from Yama, the third being the teaching about what happens after death and the imperishable self.

name: Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad
summary: A verse Upaniṣad of the Atharvaveda in three muṇḍakas that distinguishes the “lower” knowledge (the four Vedas and six Vedāṅgas) from the “higher” knowledge of the imperishable, taught by Aṅgiras to Śaunaka.
details: Opens with a transmission line: Brahmā → Atharvan → Aṅgir → Satyavāha Bhāradvāja → Aṅgiras, whom the householder Śaunaka approaches (1.1.1–3). 3.1.1 reuses RV 1.164.20 (“two birds, companions …”), and 3.1.6 contains “satyam eva jayate”, the motto of the Republic of India.

name: Praśna Upaniṣad
summary: A prose Upaniṣad of the Atharvaveda in which six students — among them Sukeśā Bhāradvāja, Satyakāma Śaibya and Kausalya Āśvalāyana — put six questions to the sage Pippalāda.
details: Note: its Satyakāma Śaibya (1.1) is a different figure from Satyakāma Jābāla of the Chāndogya.

name: Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad
summary: The shortest principal Upaniṣad (twelve verses), which identifies the syllable Om with all that is, past, present and future, and the self (ātman) with brahman, analysed into four states (waking, dream, deep sleep and the “fourth”).
details: Verse 2: “sarvaṃ hy etad brahmāyam ātmā brahma” (verified). Gauḍapāda’s Māṇḍūkya Kārikā is the earliest surviving systematic Advaita treatise; the authenticity of the commentary on it ascribed to Śaṅkara is questioned.

name: Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad
summary: A theistic verse Upaniṣad in six chapters that proclaims one Rudra, called Śiva and Maheśvara, as creator and lord, using Sāṃkhya and Yoga vocabulary; it is the earliest text to make Rudra–Śiva the supreme god and closes with the word bhakti.
details: Verified verses: 3.2 (“eko hi rudro na dvitīyāya tasthe”), 3.4, 3.5–6 (reusing Śatarudriya mantras), 3.11 (“sarvagataḥ śivaḥ”), 3.15 (= RV 10.90.2), 3.16 (paralleled in Bhagavad Gītā 13.13), 4.10 (māyā and the māyin Maheśvara), 4.21–22 (4.22 = RV 1.114.8), 5.2 (the seer Kapila), 6.16 (saṃsāra and mokṣa), 6.21 (the sage Śvetāśvatara) and 6.23 (supreme bhakti to god and teacher).

dates.label: last few centuries BCE (Olivelle’s group of verse Upaniṣads; numeric range approximate)
dates.basis: relative chronology (verse Upaniṣads later than the prose BU/CU); numbers approximate Olivelle’s “last few centuries BCE”

name: Aṣṭādhyāyī of Pāṇini
summary: Pāṇini’s grammar of Sanskrit in nearly 4,000 sūtras arranged in eight chapters, describing both the spoken language of his time and Vedic usage; it is an external, datable witness to names and cults of its period, including Vāsudeva and Arjuna (4.3.98).
details: Sūtra 4.3.98 “vāsudeva-arjunābhyāṃ vun” (verified) forms derivatives meaning “one whose bhakti is Vāsudeva / Arjuna” under the heading 4.3.95 “bhaktiḥ”; it is widely cited as the earliest reference to devotion to Vāsudeva. Pāṇini also cites earlier grammarians (e.g. Śākalya, 1.1.16).

dates.label: c. 5th – mid-4th c. BCE (not later than the early-to-mid 4th c. BCE)
dates.basis: internal linguistic and historical evidence

dates.label: c. mid-4th c. BCE or later (terminus post quem c. 350 BCE)
dates.basis: history of writing and numismatic arguments (von Hinüber, Falk), accepted by Bronkhorst

name: Mahābhāṣya of Patañjali
summary: Patañjali’s “Great Commentary” on Pāṇini and Kātyāyana’s vārttikas (c. mid-2nd c. BCE), whose example sentences incidentally attest the Kṛṣṇa–Kaṃsa story, its performance by actors (śobhikas), devotees of Vāsudeva, and contemporary events.
details: Verified in Kielhorn’s text (GRETIL): on P. 3.1.26 — “kaṃsavadham ācaṣṭe kaṃsaṃ ghātayati, balibandham ācaṣṭe baliṃ bandhayati”; śobhikas “before one’s eyes have Kaṃsa killed and Bali bound”; paintings show the blows; those who present the story (granthikas) are seen divided into “kaṃsabhaktāḥ” and “vāsudevabhaktāḥ” (Kielhorn II 34.14–36.21). On 3.2.111 — “jaghāna kaṃsaṃ kila vāsudevaḥ” and “aruṇad yavanaḥ sāketam / madhyamikām”. On 3.2.123 — “iha puṣyamitraṃ yājayāmaḥ”. On 2.2.24 — “saṅkarṣaṇadvitīyasya balaṃ kṛṣṇasya vardhatām”. On 2.2.34 — music “prāsāde dhanapati-rāma-keśavānām”. On 5.3.99 — images (arcā) set up by the Mauryas for gain. The GRETIL file lacks the commentary on adhyāya 4, so Patañjali’s remark on 4.3.98 was not checked.

dates.label: c. mid-2nd c. BCE
dates.basis: internal references to Puṣyamitra’s sacrifice and Yavana sieges of Sāketa and Madhyamikā

dates.label: late Maurya period (321–185 BCE)
dates.basis: alternative reading of the internal evidence

limits: Grammatical examples show that the Kṛṣṇa–Kaṃsa and Bali stories were known and performed in the 2nd c. BCE; they do not date the events narrated.

name: Nirukta of Yāska
summary: Yāska’s explanatory commentary on the Nighaṇṭu word-lists, the oldest surviving work of Vedic exegesis, which records rival schools of interpretation — the etymologists (nairuktas) and the “historians” (aitihāsikas).
details: Verified examples: 2.16 — “What is Vṛtra? A cloud, say the nairuktas; an asura, son of Tvaṣṭṛ, say the aitihāsikas”; 7.5 — the nairuktas hold there are only three deities: Agni (earth), Vāyu or Indra (mid-region) and Sūrya (sky); 12.1 — competing identifications of the Aśvins; 12.10 — the itihāsa of Saraṇyū, Yama and Yamī and the birth of the Aśvins and Manu.

dates.label: c. 6th–5th c. BCE (generally placed before Pāṇini)
dates.basis: relative chronology with Pāṇini

name: Indra
summary: The most frequently praised god of the Ṛgveda (about 250 hymns, roughly a quarter), the soma-drinking warrior who wields the vajra and slays Vṛtra to release the waters; in the Upaniṣads, epics and Purāṇas he remains king of the gods but loses supremacy and is often humbled.
details:
Ṛgvedic profile: slayer of Vṛtra (RV 1.32), breaker of the Vala cave with the Aṅgirases, patron of the Bharata king Sudās in the Battle of the Ten Kings (RV 7.18, 7.33), sender of Saramā (RV 10.108). RV 10.86 refrains “viśvasmād indra uttaraḥ” (Indra above all). Yāska (Nirukta 7.5) records the view that Vāyu or Indra is the single god of the middle region.

Shift of prominence: in the Kena Upaniṣad (3–4) Indra cannot grasp the mysterious being and learns from Umā Haimavatī that it is brahman, though he is then called foremost of the gods for coming nearest; in the Chāndogya (8.7–12) he is a patient pupil of Prajāpati for 101 years. In epic and Purāṇic narrative he is the ruler of svarga and the guardian of the east, repeatedly threatened, cursed or displaced (e.g. the guilt of killing Vṛtra; the Govardhana episode of the Bhāgavata, where Kṛṣṇa turns the cowherds from Indra’s worship). Hymn counts are approximate (Macdonell 1897; Jamison & Brereton 2014) and depend on how shared hymns are counted.

name: Agni
summary: The sacrificial fire as god — messenger between gods and humans, divine hotṛ and purohita — praised in about 200 Ṛgvedic hymns, including the first (RV 1.1); central to all Vedic ritual and still present in every Hindu rite.
details: The family books 2–7 open with Agni hymns, as does the whole Ṛgveda (“agnim īḻe purohitaṃ”, RV 1.1.1). The Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa (1.4.1.10–17) narrates Agni Vaiśvānara burning eastward from the Sarasvatī to the Sadānīrā with Videgha Māthava. In the Kena (3.3–6) Agni Jātavedas cannot burn a straw before brahman. Later he becomes guardian of the south-east and a secondary figure in sectarian theology while remaining indispensable in ritual. Hymn counts are approximate (Macdonell 1897; Jamison & Brereton 2014) and depend on how shared hymns are counted.

sources.quote: agnim īḻe purohitaṁ yajñasya devam ṛtvijam

name: Soma
summary: The pressed ritual drink and its god, praised in about 120 Ṛgvedic hymns, including all 114 hymns of maṇḍala 9 to Soma Pavamāna (“self-purifying”); in later tradition Soma is identified with the Moon and becomes ancestor of the Lunar dynasty.
details: The identity of the original soma plant is unknown and debated. The identification of Soma with the Moon is already Vedic (late Saṃhitā and Brāhmaṇa texts) and becomes standard; Purāṇic genealogies trace the Candravaṃśa (`lin:chandravamsha`) from Soma through Budha and Purūravas. Hymn counts are approximate (Macdonell 1897; Jamison & Brereton 2014) and depend on how shared hymns are counted.

attributes.approx. RV hymns: ≈120 (all 114 of maṇḍala 9 plus a few elsewhere)

sources.locator: RV 9.1–9.114 (114 hymns counted in the e-text)

openQuestions: Botanical identity of soma (ephedra, a mushroom and other candidates are argued).

name: Varuṇa
summary: The sovereign Āditya of the Ṛgveda who guards cosmic and moral order (ṛta), sees all and binds wrongdoers with his fetters; praised alone in about a dozen hymns and often with Mitra. Later he declines to lord of the waters and guardian of the west.
details: Varuṇa is the deity of the Vasiṣṭha hymns of contrition (RV 7.86–89) and the god who releases the bound Śunaḥśepa (RV 1.24.12–13); in the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa he grants Hariścandra a son and then claims him. RV 7.33.11 makes Vasiṣṭha a son of Mitra and Varuṇa (maitrāvaruṇa). In Taittirīya Upaniṣad 3.1 he teaches his son Bhṛgu about brahman. With RV 2.27.1 he is one of the Ādityas, sons of Aditi. In the epics and Purāṇas his ethical sovereignty fades and he becomes ruler of the ocean and the waters. Hymn counts are approximate (Macdonell 1897; Jamison & Brereton 2014) and depend on how shared hymns are counted.

name: Mitra
summary: An Āditya personifying alliance and contract, almost always paired with Varuṇa; only one Ṛgvedic hymn (RV 3.59) is addressed to him alone. He is cognate with Iranian Mithra.
details: With Varuṇa he is named father of Vasiṣṭha and (by tradition) Agastya (RV 7.33.10–13). Mitra, Varuṇa, Indra and the Nāsatyas (Aśvins) are invoked as divine witnesses in a Mitanni treaty of the 14th c. BCE — an important external attestation that belongs to the material agent’s domain (no entity yet). Hymn counts are approximate (Macdonell 1897; Jamison & Brereton 2014) and depend on how shared hymns are counted.

name: Sūrya
summary: The Sun as god, praised in about ten Ṛgvedic hymns (e.g. RV 1.50, 1.115); closely related solar deities include Savitṛ, addressed in the Gāyatrī (RV 3.62.10). Sūrya later becomes the focus of Saura worship and of great temples such as Konark.
details: Note on identity: in the Ṛgveda Savitṛ (“impeller”) and Sūrya are distinct names with overlapping functions; the registry lists Savitṛ under Sūrya as “related”, and the Gāyatrī (to Savitṛ) is linked here with that caution. RV 5.40.6–9 tells how Atri found the Sun hidden by the darkness of Svarbhānu. Hymn counts are approximate (Macdonell 1897; Jamison & Brereton 2014) and depend on how shared hymns are counted.

name: Uṣas
summary: The goddess Dawn, daughter of heaven, celebrated in about twenty of the most admired Ṛgvedic hymns (e.g. RV 1.113); she has little independent cult in later Hinduism.
details: In the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa (7.16) the bound Śunaḥśepa is finally released while praising Uṣas. Hymn counts are approximate (Macdonell 1897; Jamison & Brereton 2014) and depend on how shared hymns are counted.

sources.edition: TITUS, on the basis of Aufrecht 1879

name: Rudra
summary: A fierce Ṛgvedic archer-god of storms, disease and healing, addressed in only about three hymns (RV 1.114, 2.33, 7.46), who through the Yajurvedic Śatarudrīya and the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad becomes the supreme god Śiva.
details: Ṛgveda: RV 2.33 asks him to spare and heal; he is “lord of this world” (īśāna, 2.33.9) and father of the Maruts. Brāhmaṇas: the gods leave him behind when they go to heaven by sacrifice (ŚB 1.7.3.1, “Vāstavya”); the new-born Kumāra receives eight names — Rudra, Sarva (Śarva), Paśupati, Ugra, Aśani, Bhava, Mahān Deva, Īśāna — as forms of Agni (ŚB 6.1.3.7–18). Taittirīya Saṃhitā 4.5 (Śatarudrīya) pays homage to him in hundreds of forms and includes “namaḥ śivāya ca śivatarāya ca” (4.5.8.1). The Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad (3–4) proclaims the one Rudra, called śiva and maheśvara, as creator and lord of all. Śaiva traditions identify Rudra with Śiva; historians describe a gradual convergence of Rudra with other, non-Vedic elements (Kramrisch; Chakravarti). Hymn counts are approximate (Macdonell 1897; Jamison & Brereton 2014) and depend on how shared hymns are counted.
